clinicalPearls: The commonest benign breast condition, reflecting an aberration of normal development and involution rather than a true disease.
Presents with cyclical breast pain, nodularity and lumpiness, typically most marked in the upper outer quadrants and worse premenstrually.
Affects women predominantly in the reproductive years, with symptoms usually settling after the menopause.
Histology encompasses cysts, apocrine metaplasia, stromal fibrosis, adenosis and variable epithelial hyperplasia.
Management is largely reassurance, a well-supporting bra and simple analgesia once malignancy has been excluded by triple assessment.
Cancer risk is stratified by the epithelial component: non-proliferative change confers no excess risk, whereas atypical hyperplasia raises risk substantially.
Discrete dominant lumps or focal areas warrant imaging and core biopsy rather than being attributed to generalised nodularity.
Evening primrose oil and dietary caffeine reduction are commonly tried, though evidence for benefit is limited.
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrocystic change results from an exaggerated but physiological response of breast tissue to cyclical ovarian hormones across the reproductive years and to the involutional processes that follow. Relative imbalance in oestrogen and progesterone influence, together with variable local tissue sensitivity, produces a mixture of cyst formation from dilated lobular acini, apocrine metaplasia, fibrous stromal proliferation, adenosis and differing degrees of epithelial hyperplasia. These coexisting elements account for the lumpiness, nodularity and cyclical discomfort, and their proliferative or atypical nature determines any associated increase in subsequent carcinoma risk.
additionalDifferentials: Sclerosing adenosis presenting as a mass
additionalInvestigations: Clinical breast examination correlated with menstrual timing
Ultrasound of focal or dominant areas
Mammography in women of screening age
Core biopsy of any discrete or suspicious lesion
Cyst aspiration where symptomatic cysts are present
Pain chart to document the cyclical pattern of mastalgia
Histological grading of the epithelial component when biopsied
redFlags: A discrete, hard or fixed dominant mass within nodular tissue
Bloody or persistent single-duct nipple discharge
Skin dimpling, nipple retraction or peau d'orange
Histological finding of atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia
Progressive non-cyclical pain localised to one site
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, with symptoms typically easing after the menopause. Long-term breast cancer risk depends on the underlying histology, being negligible for non-proliferative change and appreciably higher where atypical hyperplasia is found.
pitfalls: Attributing a discrete dominant lump to generalised nodularity and omitting biopsy
Failing to recognise that atypical hyperplasia carries a materially increased cancer risk
Labelling the change a 'disease', which causes unnecessary anxiety
Overlooking hormone replacement therapy as a cause of persistent symptoms after the menopause
Reassuring on the basis of imaging alone when clinical findings are discordant
references: Standard textbook of benign breast disease and the ANDI classification
National guidance on benign breast conditions
management: Provide reassurance once triple assessment excludes malignancy, framing the condition as an aberration of normal development and involution
Offer supportive measures including a well-fitting supportive bra, simple analgesia and topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for mastalgia
Use a pain chart to document the cyclical pattern of mastalgia and guide treatment of persistent symptoms
Aspirate symptomatic cysts, sending any bloodstained aspirate for cytology and reassessing any residual mass
Reserve hormonal therapy such as danazol or tamoxifen for severe refractory cyclical mastalgia under specialist supervision
Perform core biopsy of discrete or suspicious lesions with risk-stratified surveillance where atypical hyperplasia is found
Refer to breast surgery for dominant or persistent lumps and any diagnostic uncertainty
